scenes.visual: Title card 'Same Protein, Different Switch' on a pale sea-green background. COLOUR MAP for both films: the marine fish and anything marine are BLUE; the Paxton Lake fish and anything Paxton are ORANGE; Pitx1 RNA is GOLD; Pitx1 protein is a PURPLE blob; DNA is a charcoal ribbon; enhancers are small rectangular switch tabs sitting on the DNA, each labelled with its tissue. The pelvis is always drawn the same way: a small bony girdle on the belly carrying a pair of long spines. All fish are flat side-view cartoons, not photographs.

scenes.tts: This lake stickleback has almost no pelvis, yet its Pit ex one protein is unchanged. So what broke, if the protein did not? The likely answer is a kind of switch.
scenes.caption: This lake stickleback has almost no pelvis, yet its Pitx1 protein is unchanged. So what broke, if the protein did not? The likely answer is a kind of switch.
scenes.visual: An ORANGE cartoon stickleback swims in from the right with a bare belly where the pelvis should be. Above it a PURPLE protein blob labelled 'Pitx1 protein' gets a green tick and the word 'unchanged'. A large question mark pulses between the fish and the protein.
scenes.narration: This lake stickleback has almost no pelvis, yet its Pitx1 protein is unchanged. So what broke, if the protein did not? The likely answer is a kind of switch.

scenes.tts: Marine sticklebacks carry a pelvis: a bony girdle with a pair of long spines. It is the fish's version of your hips and legs. In Paxton Lake, British Columbia, the bottom-feeding fish have a greatly reduced pelvis. Most have no pelvic bones at all.
scenes.visual: A BLUE marine stickleback swims in from the left and stops beside the ORANGE fish. Its pelvis (girdle plus two long spines) glows white and gets the label 'pelvis'. A faint human hip-and-leg outline appears beside it with a dotted line linking the two, labelled 'same ancestral structure'. Then the ORANGE fish's belly is outlined: only a small stub remains, labelled 'Paxton Lake benthic: greatly reduced'. A small map pin reads 'Paxton Lake, British Columbia'. A second ORANGE fish swims past with no pelvic bones at all, labelled 'most: none'.
scenes.narration: Marine sticklebacks carry a pelvis: a bony girdle with a pair of long spines. It is the fish's version of your hips and legs. In Paxton Lake, British Columbia, the bottom-feeding fish have a greatly reduced pelvis. Most have no pelvic bones at all.

scenes.tts: The gene most strongly tied to that difference is Pit ex one. Its protein is a transcription factor. It binds DNA and switches other genes on or off. In the lake fish examined, that protein was unchanged.
scenes.caption: The gene most strongly tied to that difference is Pitx1. Its protein is a transcription factor. It binds DNA and switches other genes on or off. In the lake fish examined, that protein was unchanged.
scenes.visual: Zoom into a charcoal DNA ribbon. A long block labelled 'Pitx1: protein-coding part' sits in the middle. A protein blob pops off it, lands on another stretch of DNA, and a small downstream gene lights up, labelled 'switches other genes on or off'. Two protein chains, one BLUE and one ORANGE, slide together and their amino-acid beads match one for one; a stamp reads 'same encoded protein (fish examined)'. Do not show DNA letters matching.
scenes.narration: The gene most strongly tied to that difference is Pitx1. Its protein is a transcription factor. It binds DNA and switches other genes on or off. In the lake fish examined, that protein was unchanged.

scenes.tts: Pit ex one is not only a pelvis gene. It is also used in the jaw. Mice with no working Pit ex one die, and they have malformed hind limbs among other defects.
scenes.caption: Pitx1 is not only a pelvis gene. It is also used in the jaw. Mice with no working Pitx1 die, and they have malformed hind limbs among other defects.
scenes.visual: A cartoon fish larva in side view. GOLD light appears in its jaw, then in the pelvic region on the belly, labelled 'Pitx1 used here'. A small inset cartoon mouse appears with a grey X over the Pitx1 protein and tags: 'hind limbs malformed', 'other defects', 'does not survive'.
scenes.narration: Pitx1 is not only a pelvis gene. It is also used in the jaw. Mice with no working Pitx1 die, and they have malformed hind limbs among other defects.

scenes.tts: Suppose the lake fish had broken the protein itself. Where would you expect the damage to show?
scenes.visual: The ORANGE coding block gets a red X. The larva sits below it with GOLD Pitx1 RNA still shown in the jaw and the pelvic region; a small PURPLE protein blob over each region turns grey and misshapen, with a question mark over each. On-screen text: 'Broken protein: where is the damage?'
scenes.narration: Suppose the lake fish had broken the protein itself. Where would you expect the damage to show?

scenes.visual: Hold the larva with two question marks. A small countdown ring fills over five seconds.

scenes.tts: Everywhere the gene works. A protein with no function would fail in the jaw and the pelvis at once. The mouse shows how costly that can be. The lake fish do not look like that.
scenes.visual: With the red X still on the coding block, GOLD Pitx1 RNA stays visible in both the jaw and the pelvic region of the larva, but the grey protein blobs there do nothing: the small downstream genes they should switch on stay dark in both regions, and both regions get red outlines, labelled 'RNA made, protein does not work'. Do not make GOLD vanish: a coding mutation does not remove the gene's RNA. Then the picture splits: on the right, the real ORANGE lake fish appears with GOLD in its mouth and lower jaw, labelled 'Pitx1 RNA kept in mouth and lower jaw'. A banner reads 'not a broken protein'.
scenes.narration: Everywhere the gene works. A protein with no function would fail in the jaw and the pelvis at once. The mouse shows how costly that can be. The lake fish do not look like that.

scenes.tts: The way out is an enhancer. An enhancer is a short stretch of noncoding DNA that switches a gene on in particular tissues. One gene can have several. One can serve the jaw, another the pelvis. Their jobs can overlap.
scenes.visual: Back to the DNA ribbon. The red X fades from the coding block. Two switch tabs grow out of the DNA beside the gene, labelled 'jaw switch' and 'pelvic switch', with the label 'enhancer: noncoding DNA'. As each tab flips up, a GOLD wire runs to the larva below and lights the matching region: first the jaw, then the pelvis.
scenes.narration: The way out is an enhancer. An enhancer is a short stretch of noncoding DNA that switches a gene on in particular tissues. One gene can have several. One can serve the jaw, another the pelvis. Their jobs can overlap.

scenes.tts: So where is Pit ex one RNA in a lake fish larva? A labelled probe pairs with the RNA and leaves a gold mark wherever it is. In Paxton larvae, gold sits in the mouth and lower jaw. Where the pelvis forms, there is none.
scenes.caption: So where is Pitx1 RNA in a lake fish larva? A labelled probe pairs with the RNA and leaves a gold mark wherever it is. In Paxton larvae, gold sits in the mouth and lower jaw. Where the pelvis forms, there is none.
scenes.visual: An ORANGE-outlined Paxton larva on a white dish. A small probe strand drifts in and zips onto a GOLD RNA strand, labelled 'probe pairs with Pitx1 RNA'. GOLD stain then blooms over the mouth and lower jaw only. A dashed circle on the belly, labelled 'where the pelvis forms', stays empty. Small tag: 'in situ hybridization, Paxton larva (corrected 2006 figures)'.
scenes.narration: So where is Pitx1 RNA in a lake fish larva? A labelled probe pairs with the RNA and leaves a gold mark wherever it is. In Paxton larvae, gold sits in the mouth and lower jaw. Where the pelvis forms, there is none.

scenes.tts: So suppose the jaw switch still works, but the pelvic switch does not. Then that body part shrinks, while the gene keeps its other jobs.
scenes.visual: A small tag 'hypothesis' appears; only after the word 'suppose', on the DNA, the ORANGE 'pelvic switch' tab cracks and falls flat; the 'jaw switch' tab stays up with its GOLD wire lit. Below, the adult ORANGE fish: GOLD in the jaw, an empty belly. Side by side, the BLUE fish keeps both switches up and both GOLD regions lit.
scenes.narration: So suppose the jaw switch still works, but the pelvic switch does not. Then that body part shrinks, while the gene keeps its other jobs.

scenes.tts: Compare the two fish once more. Both make the same Pit ex one protein. Both use it in the jaw. Of the tissues compared, only the pelvic use differs. The pelvic use changed, and the jaw use was spared. Other tissues were not all checked.
scenes.visual: Split screen. Left, the BLUE marine fish; right, the ORANGE Paxton fish. A checklist builds between them, one row at a time, with ticks for both: 'same Pitx1 protein', 'GOLD in the jaw'. The third row, 'GOLD in the pelvis', gets a tick for BLUE and an empty box for ORANGE, while the ORANGE pelvis outline fades. A small footnote tag: 'tissues compared: jaw and pelvis'.
scenes.caption: Compare the two fish once more. Both make the same Pitx1 protein. Both use it in the jaw. Of the tissues compared, only the pelvic use differs. The pelvic use changed, and the jaw use was spared. Other tissues were not all checked.
scenes.narration: Compare the two fish once more. Both make the same Pitx1 protein. Both use it in the jaw. Of the tissues compared, only the pelvic use differs. The pelvic use changed, and the jaw use was spared. Other tissues were not all checked.

scenes.tts: This is the best-studied route to a reduced pelvis in sticklebacks. It is not the only one. A missing gold mark also leaves a question open. Is the break in this gene's own DNA, or in another gene?
scenes.visual: The two fish shrink to the top of the screen. Two labelled arrows point at the broken switch: one to 'the Pitx1 copy's own DNA?' and one to 'another gene that supplies its regulators?'. A small tag reads 'best-studied route, not the only one'.
scenes.narration: This is the best-studied route to a reduced pelvis in sticklebacks. It is not the only one. A missing gold mark also leaves a question open. Is the break in this gene's own DNA, or in another gene?

scenes.visual: End card with the logo hexagon. Line: 'Evolution changed where Pitx1 is used, not what it makes.'
